caseno: Civil Appeal No. 6 of 1975 from Civil Revision No. 127 of 1969.
lawyer: M.H. Khandokar, Senior Advocate instructed by S. M. Huq, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Appellant. S.R. Pal, Senior Advocate, instructed by Abdur Rab II. Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Syed Ahmed Molla ------ Appellant
Vs. 
Halima Begum and others  ------ Respondent.
full_judgment:
Mahmud Husain C. J.—This arm by special leave is against the judgment of a Bench of the High Court in a miscellaneous case arising out of an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951, seeking pre-emption of certain land sold by Khan Brothers, by a registered kabala dated 3rd December, 1966 to Muhammad Khalilur Rahman, respondent No. 4 for a consideration of Taka 6000.00 This application at the instance of the appellant was subsequently treated to be an application for pre-emption under scion 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

2. The appellant alleged that he is a co-sharer by purchase in the holding recorded in C. S. khatian No. 39 which corresponds to S. A. khatain No. 34 of mouza Debnagar, P.S Daulatpur and respondent No. 2 is another co-sharer in the same holding.

Respondents 1, 3, 4 and 5 are strangers to the holding Respondent No. 2 with notice to the appellant transferred the land which is the subject matter of the miscellaneous case to respondent No. 1 by a registered kabala dated 3.12.66. It is the case of the appellant that he is a co-sharer by purchase in respect of the boding recorded in C. S Khatiant No. 39 corresponding to S. A. Khatian No. 34 of mouza Debnagar and that on 3.12.66 respondent No. 5 Khan Brothers sold away the disputed land measuring about .90½ acre appertaining to the said holding to a stranger, namely, respondent No. 4 Muhammad Khalilur Rahman. The appellant was served with a notice of transfer on 8.12.66 and as such he was entitled to preempt the said land.

3. Respondent No. 3 and 4 contested the miscellaneous case on the ground that the appellant is not a co-sherer in the holding and the notice served upon him would not operate as an estoppel against them.

4. The trial court found that the appellant is not a Co-sharer in holding and the service of notice on the appellant will not operate as estoppel against them and accordingly dismissed the application for preemption. The appellant preferred an appeal and the learned Additional District Judge set aside the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge and allowed the appellants application for pre-emption. As against that there was a regional application before the High Court and the learned Judges of the High Court set aside the judgment and we, passed by the Additional District Judge and retired that of the learned Subordinate Judge dismissing the application for preemption. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court in the exercise of its power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure acted on correct principle in the exercise of jurisdiction in disturbing the are appellate court's finding of fact that the appellant is a co-sharer tenant.

5. Mr. M. H. Khondker, learned Counsel for the appellant in support of the appeal submitted that the lands in C. S. plot Nos. 1202 and 1203 along with six other plots (1204 to 1209 were recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 39 of mouza Debnagar, P.S Daulatpur, District Khulna in the name of Ujiruddin Nayan Shaikh and Abdus Samad Shaikh in equal shares as under raiytas with right of occupancy under the raiyati recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 38 of the said mouza. The said two plots namely, 1202 and 1203, were recorded in possession of Abdus Sarnad and the said C. S. Khatinus were finally published on 13.5.1927. Delwar Shaikh alias Delwar Hosszin alias Dolwar Ahmed, brother of the recorded tenant Abdus Samad and husband of Sakhina alias Rokeya or Salhina or Rabeya, was in possession of the aforesaid lands and being in such possession claimed the land to be his and sold the same along with some other lands to the appellant in consideration by a registered kabala dated 21.4.1951, and put the appellant in possession thereof, and since then the appellant has been in peaceful possession by making certain pucca constructions, and on payment of rents along with his co-sharer tenants to the landlord and thereafter to the Government after the acquisition of the Rent-receiving interest by the Government Preparation of record of rights was started under the provisions of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and the aforesaid two plots had been corded in the preliminary stage in the name of Sultan Shaikh, son of late Nayan Shaikh. The appellant fled objection for correction of record on 1.8.60 making the said Delwar Shaikh as preform defendant thereto and asserted that he has been in possession of the said two plots of land, 1202 and 1203, by purchase from Delwar Shaikh. The Assistant Settlement Officer by the judgment and order dated 29.8.60 recorded the appellant's name after striking out of the name of Sultan Shaikh. Thereafter record of rights (being khatian No. 34) under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has been prepared and finally published in the name of the appellant and the other co-sharer tenant, Abdus Sabur Khan, who acquired the other two plots of land from the heirs of the said two c-sharer tenants, namely, Ujir Shaikh and Nayan Shaikh. It appears that the aforesaid plots of lands were not included in the said Kabala dated 21.4.51 on the basis of which the appellant claimed to be co-sharer. At this the said Delwar Hossain gave another kabala in respect of the said lands executed by his wife named Rokeya and made over a deed of relinquishment dated 1.5.36 in the name of his wife Sakhina Khatun executed by his brother, Abdus Samad Shaikh. The appellant remained in peaceful possession since 21.4.51 and neither Delwar Hossain nor Sakhina nor Rokeya nor anybody else had possessed the same, so the appellant is a co-share tenant in the holding recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 39, now S. A. Katina No. 34, While the appellant and the said Khan Brothers were the recorded co-sharer tenants in the holding, the co-sharer Khalil Brothers sold their share by a registered kabala dated 3.12.66 to a stranger, Md. Khalilur Rahman, Respondent No. 4, for consideration of Taka 6,000.00. The appellant was served with the notice of this transfer on 8.12.66 and thereupon he made an application for preemption as stated earlier.

6. It appears that the courts below made a wrong approach of the case when they were dealing with the point as to whether Sakhina and Rokeya is the same person. It should be noted that the appellant's purchase was on 21.4.51 and he was inducted into possession. The whole approach of the case should have been from a question as to whether the 4ppeliant is a co-sharer and entitled to pre-empt the land of the kabala dated 1.72.66.  There is a recital in the kabala under preemption to the effect that the appellant is a co-sharer. So, from the recital in the kabala we get a clear admission by respondents that the appellant is a co-sharer in the holding to which the case land appertains. There is similar recital in Exhibit 3 dated 16.2.63. Which relates to the C.S. Khatian No. 39 a reference to the Mukti Patra dated 1.5.36, Exhibit 4, which appears to have been executed by Abdus Samad in favour of Sakhina Khatun, wife of Dildar Shaikh show that the executant admitted that he had Do right title and' interest in the land but it appertains to the recipient Sakhina Khatun and that he was the benamdar of Sakhina Khatun.

7. Now the kabala in favour of the appellant was executed by Dildar on 21.4.51 and pursuant to the said deed at was inducted into possession. The fact that the appellant has been described as co-sharer in the kabala executed by Khan Brothers and notice on him as co-sharer was served and the very fact that the appellant remained in undisturbed possession of his purchased land from 1951 and the S.A. Khatian was prepared in the name of the appellant, it is needless to determine whether Rokeya or Rabeya is Sakhin a Since the appellant purchased from a Abdus Samad, husband of Rokeya, and when the recorded tenant in the C S. Khatian never claimed any right in the suit land and this point was finally concluded by the first appellate court there arises no question of illegal exercise of jurisdiction by the lower appellate court for interference by the High Court.

8. It may be mentioned that the kabala, Exhibit 3, was executed by Rokeya Khatun, wife of Md. Dildar Ahmed on 16.2.62 and, It was also signed by Dildar Sheikh and it Contains a reference of Muktipatra dated 1.5.36. Asserted by Rokeya Khatun that the Muktipatra was in her favour Executed on 1.5.1936 being No. 2803 for the year 1936 registered in Book No. 1 Volume No. 27 at pages 62-63. This specific reference of the Muktipatra in the kabala, Exhibit 3, leaves no room for consideration as to whether Sakhina or Rabeya or Rokeya is the recipient of the Muktipatra. The learned Additional District Judge quoting apportion relating to Muktipatra in the judgment made elaborate discussion and in our view it left on room. For the High Court to consider or examine when there Rokeya was Sakhina or Rabeya. This conclusion arrived at by the learned Additional District Judge cannot be interfered within Revision al jurisdiction by the High Court. In Order to exercise jurisdiction under section 115 Of the code or Civet  procedure it must appear that the Subordinate Court has exercised its jurisdiction not vested in it by law or failed to exercise a jurisdiction vested in it by law or acted in exercise of its jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity. The present case cannot be brought within the purview of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure since the question whether the appellant is a co-sharer tenant or not is a question of fact.

9. The case of Joy Chand Lal Babu v. Kamalaksha Chaudhury and others (1) 53 C. W. N. (P. C.) 562 dealt with a loan and question arose for determination as to whether it was a commercial loan within the meaning of the Bengal Money-Lenders Act, 1940 and the High Court disagreeing with the lower appellate court held that the loan was not a commercial loan and set aside the order. So the High Court had power to interfere in revision under subsection (b) of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure inasmuch as the subordinate court invested itself with a jurisdiction which in law it did not possess. So this case cannot be of any assistance in support of the contention of Mr. Pal, the learned counsel for the respondents.

10. The case of N.S. Venkatagiri Awangar and another V. The Hindu Religious End-women's Board, Madras (2) 53. C.W.N.(PC) 458 relates to construction of a will of a testator on the question as to whether the temple was private or public. It has been found by their Lordships of the Privy Council that the High Court was not justified in interfering in revision under subsection (c) of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. So this case also cannot be of any assistance for Mr. Pal.

<u>11. In the case of Ramjan Khan alias Ramjan Allas Khan v. Obaklul Huq Chowdhury and other, (3) 28 D.L.R (AD) 57 conclusion arrived at on the issue of exercise of jurisdiction Under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure runs as follows:-</u>

<u>"We may conclude that the High Court exercising its provisional jurisdiction under 115 C.P.C. cannot interfere with the decision of the subordinate court, unless it has exercised its jurisdiction not conferred by law or has failed to exercise jurisdiction so conferred upon it, or has acted illegally in the exercise of jurisdiction which means that it has committed a breach of some provision of law or with material irregularity in the exercise of its jurisdiction which means that it has committed some error of procedure during the course of trial and this breach or error has affected its ultimate exercise of jurisdiction. Except within this narrow he High Court has no power to interfere conclusion of the subordinate court either on a question of law or fact ho infers profoundly it may differ with the subordinate court."</u>

<u>"Mr. Pal cannot find any support from this observation as made above in the case. The present case does not come within the purview of any of the three categories as enunciated earlier to invoke the aid from section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The intention of the Legislature is manifest from section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure that the order of the subordinate court whether right or wrong shall be final unless such decision can b: brought within the three condition provided in the said section the learned Judge of the High Court erred in interfering with the judgment of the first appellate court in revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

12. In the result, the appeal is allowed with costs. The judgment and order of the High Court are set aside and those of the Additional District Judge are restored.

End.
